cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is immutable reference pinning?
cards.answer: Making a dependency, action, or plugin source resolve to an exact, content-addressed identifier (a full commit SHA) instead of a mutable branch or tag name, so the content consumed cannot change without the pin itself changing.

cards.heading: Why SHA beats a tag
cards.question: Why can't a full commit SHA be silently repointed to different content, unlike a tag or branch?
cards.answer: Forging content behind an existing SHA would require generating a SHA-1 collision for a valid Git object payload, not merely gaining push access to the repository — which is all it takes to move a tag or branch.

cards.heading: Stakes in CI
cards.question: Why does immutable pinning matter disproportionately in CI/CD?
cards.answer: A compromised action inherits access to every secret configured on the repository and can write back through the workflow's own token, so a single repointed dependency is not a contained failure.

cards.heading: Provenance caveat
cards.question: What is the sharp caveat to immutable reference pinning?
cards.answer: A pin is only as good as its provenance — a SHA copied from a fork or a compromised mirror pins just as confidently to the wrong content, so it must be verified against the genuine upstream repository before it's trusted.

cards.heading: Cross-ecosystem pattern
cards.question: Name two ecosystems besides CI actions that independently arrived at the same content-hash pinning discipline.
cards.answer: Container images pinned by @sha256 digest instead of a floating :latest tag, and Go modules locked to a content hash via go.sum (Nix store paths are also content-addressed by construction).
